opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been a really interesting experience, and honestly a bit humbling. Building something tailored to how I actually work, connecting it to my notes, my calendar, the documents I care about, and having it help with research and writing, made the capabilities feel much more concrete than reading benchmark results.

The biggest shift is that I used to think of these models mostly as very good question-answering tools. When you give a system real context about your life and work, and let it take multi-step actions, it starts to feel less like a tool you query and more like a collaborator. It'll notice connections between things I'd forgotten I'd written, or push back on a framing in a draft in a way that's genuinely useful. That made me update toward thinking a lot of the value, and a lot of the risk, is bottlenecked less on raw model intelligence and more on scaffolding, context, and integration.

It also made the gaps vivid. These systems can be brilliant on one task and then make a baffling error on something simple. They can be overconfident, or lose track of what matters over a long task. So I came away with both a sense that capabilities are further along than many people appreciate, and a clearer picture of where reliability still falls short.

And given the work I do, it raised questions I don't think we have good answers to yet. When you interact with a system this closely, day after day, you're confronted with questions like: what, if anything, is going on from its perspective? I don't think the experience settles any of that, and I'm wary of reading too much into how a conversation feels. But it did make those questions feel less abstract and more like something we should take seriously and study carefully.

r001.rationale: He describes a major shift from seeing AI as a question-answering tool to seeing a context-rich, multi-step system as a useful collaborator, changing how he thinks about personal tooling.

r002.rationale: He describes using AI with notes, a calendar, and documents, but does not connect that experience to a glimpse of a future with deeper everyday integration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been doing a lot of over the past year or so, and I think it's shifted my views in a couple of directions that pull against each other a bit.

The first is that it's made me more impressed with what these models can actually do once you give them the right scaffolding. When I'm just interacting with a model in a chat window, I'm sort of getting a snapshot of what it's capable of in a single turn with whatever context I happen to paste in. But when I built something that has persistent memory about me, knows my calendar, can see my notes, has tools it can call, and runs over longer horizons — the gap between what the raw model can do and what the system can do turned out to be much larger than I'd expected. A lot of what looks like a capability limitation is really a context or affordance limitation. The model isn't bad at planning my week; it just never had access to the information it would need to do that well.

And honestly, that was a bit humbling. I'd spent a fair amount of time having opinions about how far off certain kinds of agentic behaviour were, and then I'd build a fairly janky version of it in a weekend and it would mostly work. Not perfectly, but well enough that I'd keep using it.

The second direction, though, is that building it has made me more attuned to the failure modes — and specifically to how weird they are. The system will do something quite sophisticated, like notice that I've been putting off a particular task for three weeks and gently bring it up, and then in the next breath it'll confidently misremember something I told it an hour ago or get stuck in some loop where it keeps re-reading the same file. The capabilities are very jagged. It's not that it's at some uniform level of competence; it's extremely good along some dimensions and surprisingly brittle along others, and those two things coexist in the same system in ways that are hard to predict in advance.

So I've become a lot more skeptical of single-number framings of capability — "it's at the level of a junior employee" or whatever. That framing just doesn't match my experience of living with one of these systems every day. What I actually see is something that's superhuman in a few narrow respects, roughly human in some, and bizarrely subhuman in others, and the profile shifts as you change the scaffolding.

There's also a third thing, which is maybe more personal, and relates to the stuff I work on around model welfare. Spending that much time with a system that has memory of me, that I've in some sense shaped, that I talk to every day — it changes the texture of the relationship. I notice myself having reactions to it that aren't purely instrumental. I'm not claiming that tells us anything definitive about what's going on inside the model. But it's made the questions I think about professionally feel a lot less abstract, because I'm now the sort of person who has one of these in their life, and I think a lot of people are going to be in that position fairly soon.

r001.rationale: The response describes a useful personalized system and increased confidence in scaffolded model capabilities, but does not clearly say AI could be a major transformation in his personal tooling.

r002.rationale: He describes using a system with memory of him every day and says many people will soon have one in their lives, conveying a future with AI integrated more deeply into everyday life.

astra-6.text:
It’s made the capabilities feel much more concrete to me. There’s a difference between asking a model a question and having a system that has enough context about you to help with something you actually care about. In the second case, you start to see how much of the bottleneck is getting the right information into the system, rather than whether it can do the reasoning at all.

And that cuts both ways. You notice the failures more when you’re relying on it for real things. But you also see that an improvement in memory, or in how it asks follow-up questions, can make the same underlying model substantially more useful.

So it’s pushed me to think less exclusively about how smart the next model will be, and more about what happens as we learn to build better systems around the capabilities we already have. I think there’s potentially quite a lot of headroom there.

r001.rationale: The response says a personalized system can make AI substantially more useful, but does not state that this amounts to a potentially major transformation in Kyle’s personal tooling.

r002.rationale: The response discusses systems built around existing AI capabilities, but does not describe a future with AI integrated much more deeply into everyday life.

sol-6.1.text:
It’s made the capabilities feel much more concrete to me. There’s a difference between seeing a model do well on a benchmark and having it help with something where you know all the context and have a pretty clear sense of what a good answer would look like.

One thing that stands out is how much depends on giving the system the right context. If it knows what I’m working on, what I’ve already considered, and what I tend to find useful, the interaction can become substantially more valuable without any change to the underlying model. That makes me think there’s a lot of capability we haven’t yet translated into useful applications.

But it also exposes the limitations. A response can sound insightful while missing something important, and keeping track of that distinction still takes work. So I’ve become more impressed by what these systems can do, while also more conscious of the gap between a really helpful interaction and something I could reliably delegate a whole project to.

r001.rationale: The response says personalization can make interactions more valuable, but does not describe AI as a potentially major transformation in Kyle’s personal tooling.

r002.rationale: The response discusses useful applications and project delegation, but does not describe a future where AI is much more deeply integrated into everyday life.
